readers.title: The Funnel Is Not the Frontier
readers.text: Video Deconstruction · October 16, 2026 The Funnel Is Not the Frontier What you understand, what you can access, and what you can prove are three different things. Reader brief What the video is about DevLogic narrates Karpathy's AI-use funnel and its proposed filters of ambition, jagged capability and access. It contrasts casual use with technical work and private laboratory accounts. Why you should care Useful for interpreting conflicting AI anecdotes. Watch the short framing; skip it if you need a measured census or access to confidential lab results. What GhostMesh takes away Separate competence, access and verified outcomes. Compare bounded tasks and disclose interventions rather than ranking people with unmeasured population estimates. GhostMesh verdict: Interesting, unproven . Editorial recommendation, not factual verification. Architecture impact: experiment recommended. Proposed only; no adoption implied. Share this Video Deconstruction Email Original source · DevLogic · 6:14 Video loads only when you choose to play. GhostMesh’s interpretation follows below. Karpathy: The AI Understanding Gap Is Getting Worse, Fast DevLogic · Published October 12, 2026 · 374 seconds Watch on YouTube ↗ Access can explain a gap. Evidence must establish the result. This is DevLogic’s narration about Karpathy’s thread, not Karpathy speaking. The essay below is original GhostMesh analysis, not an expanded transcript or a certification of confidential laboratory claims. Creator-provided YouTube source chapters Watch with a question. Exact source labels and times; the context beneath each is GhostMesh’s. Every chapter has an in-page seek and a direct YouTube fallback. 0:00 The sharp funnel explained Watch how the population metaphor is introduced; treat its counts as illustrative estimates. YouTube ↗ 1:18 The shallow end: chatbots and casual use Notice how product tier and prior experience shape what users can reasonably observe. YouTube ↗ 2:35 Frontier labs and agent swarms Separate narrated laboratory claims from publicly inspectable demonstrations. YouTube ↗ 3:44 Three filters: ambition, jaggedness, access Use the three filters to design a bounded experiment, rather than rank a person. YouTube ↗ 5:00 Why the AI debate goes nowhere Compare the evidence behind opposing judgments before assuming either user is dishonest. YouTube ↗ GhostMesh interpretation Knowledge / competence Access / resources Outcomes / verification Source estimates are not measured populations. Proposals below have not been run for this publication. 1. A funnel describes exposure, not a ranking of people DevLogic’s six-minute commentary makes a useful observation: people can encounter radically different AI systems and still believe they are discussing the same thing. A free chatbot, a coding agent with a repository, and a confidential laboratory workflow expose different behaviors. GhostMesh’s thesis is that the gap becomes understandable only when we separate knowledge and competence, real access, and demonstrable outcomes. None can stand in for the other two. Knowing the vocabulary does not establish practical skill; possessing a subscription does not establish a successful result. The commentary interprets Andrej Karpathy’s October 11 X thread. Its population figures are explicitly napkin math: roughly six billion barely exposed, one to two billion casual free-chat users, around twenty million professional frontier users in mathematics and code, and perhaps five thousand people with unpublished internal-lab access. There is no survey method here. These are illustrative estimates, not certified usage data or exclusive discrete census populations. Multiplying them into precise proportions would manufacture certainty the source does not supply. The useful question is therefore not where Tony or another reader ranks. It is what their observations permit them to conclude. A repeated, independently checked result on an owned task can justify a bounded capability claim. An impressive anecdote can motivate a test. Neither a confident narrator nor proximity to a laboratory converts inaccessible work into publicly audited evidence. The funnel is a prompt for investigation, not proof of an elite hierarchy. 2. Ambition changes the experiment A paragraph request usually tests fluent completion in a short interaction. A project tests whether a system can retain constraints, inspect its environment, recover from mistakes, and deliver something another person can evaluate. Problem ambition changes the surface on which capabilities become visible. Longer horizons add dependency management and error accumulation; they also give tools and feedback time to help. That is a different experiment from finding a cleverer prompt. For GhostMesh, a meaningful ambitious task might reconcile conflicting source receipts, repair a bounded repository defect, or assemble a reviewable explanation from authorized evidence. The task needs an explicit finish line. Otherwise a long-running agent can substitute activity for completion and an operator can remember the best moment while forgetting interventions. Time spent, retries, human assistance, and unresolved defects belong in the result alongside the final artifact. Ambition is also constrained by opportunity. A casual user may have no safe repository, spare compute, or permission to automate their workplace. Their limited experience is not a moral or intellectual failure. Giving everyone the biggest available problem is poor experimental advice if the failure cost is unbounded. Start with an owned problem whose answer matters, preserve a baseline, and expand the horizon only while failures remain inspectable and recoverable. 3. Jaggedness breaks the general-intelligence shortcut Coding and mathematics offer unusually useful feedback loops: programs can be executed and some claims can be checked formally. That makes them fertile environments for training, search, and agent iteration. Yet passing tests is not identical to satisfying a customer, and a plausible proof still needs mathematical scrutiny. The narrator’s explanation of reinforcement-learning incentives is a narrative about why strengths cluster, not a complete account of every model’s training. A system that repairs a digital benchmark can still misunderstand an ambiguous instruction, misread an interface, or fail to recognize whose permission matters. Broad human capability involves social context, embodied constraints, judgment under incomplete feedback, and consequences that cannot be reduced to a convenient checker. A successful coding demonstration does not measure all of those things. Conversely, a chatbot’s embarrassing everyday mistake does not erase its ability to solve a difficult, verifiable technical task. Stanford’s 2026 AI Index provides cross-context support for this unevenness: coding benchmark performance improved rapidly while OSWorld computer-use tasks still showed substantial failure. Those evaluations measure different tasks under different conditions. Their contrast supports caution about transfer, not a single ladder of intelligence. GhostMesh should describe the task, verifier, and failure distribution before reaching for a universal adjective such as capable or incapable. 4. Access matters; confidential claims remain confidential Internal laboratories can have genuinely different resources: unpublished models, larger inference budgets, specialized scaffolds, privileged datasets, and teams that know how to use them. These differences can produce real information asymmetry. It would be unreasonable to assume that public products exhaust everything a laboratory can demonstrate. It is equally unreasonable to treat a secondhand description of hidden systems as a measured public result. DevLogic narrates swarms, long projects, security work, science, and mathematics. This caption-only source does not let an outsider audit those systems, identify their interventions, inspect their scoring rules, or compare failed runs. The approximately five-thousand-person population is not independently verified here. Neither that number nor the dramatic examples establish a capability threshold or consensus among all labs. The right evidence status is unknown, with a clear route for future verification. An operator using Pro and Codex across a VPS, Hyperion, a Mac, and multiple providers can build substantial practical competence. That system design still supplies no numerical placement in Karpathy’s estimated populations and no implication of private laboratory access. GhostMesh’s defensible contribution is a documented workflow: which sources were checked, what actions were allowed, who reviewed the result, and what a receipt actually proves. Those facts can travel without borrowing someone else’s insider status. 5. More agents, more makers, and more authority are different things Orchestration changes how work is divided and checked. It does not increase the parameters of the underlying model, and it must not silently expand permissions. Ten agents sharing a mistaken source can make one error look like agreement. A second model maker can offer useful variation, but different branding does not establish independent evidence: training material, benchmarks, retrieved documents, and evaluation incentives may still be correlated. Open weights from families such as Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, and Kimi can reduce barriers to inspection, local deployment, and experimentation where suitable releases and hardware are available. They do not guarantee equivalent capability, matching guardrails, trustworthy model provenance, or membership in any imagined insider group. Stanford’s report describes a narrow U.S.–China performance gap on its comparisons; that does not imply every open checkpoint matches every hosted or unpublished system. The documented tool ecosystem is more concrete. Qwen-Agent describes function calling and agent tooling; DeepSeek documents a tool-call exchange in which the application executes functions and returns results. These are integration mechanisms, not evidence of autonomous success or permission enforcement. GhostMesh should record checkpoint identity, provider, quantization where relevant, scaffold revision, and allowed tools separately. A local deployment changes operational control; it does not automatically improve reasoning or make a retrieved instruction safe to obey. 6. Receipts make disagreement productive Two honest users can disagree because they sampled different systems, dates, tasks, budgets, and success criteria. A developer may count a working prototype as a breakthrough while a maintainer counts the review and cleanup as the expensive part. A person asking for sensitive advice may reasonably prioritize reliability over peak performance. Neither perspective becomes false because another user has a stronger demonstration in a different domain. Disagreement also reflects selection. Public success clips omit ordinary failures; a frustrated user may stop before learning a useful workflow. Experts can compensate for missing context without noticing how much guidance they supplied. Shared evidence should expose these interventions. A receipt needs the task definition, source identities, tool boundaries, output artifact, verification, cost, and human contribution. It should distinguish an attempted operation from an accepted operation and an accepted operation from a successful outcome. GhostMesh’s mission control should make those distinctions visible while preserving signer/owner-only authority and human oversight. An evidence receipt records observations; it does not grant permission. A source check supports an interpretation; it does not authorize publication. SharePlane and a public Reader can explain a finding without exposing private mission-control context. The public artifact should contain enough method to challenge the claim, while confidential inputs and credentials remain outside it. These are design requirements to demonstrate, not compliance claims established by this essay. 7. Five experiments GhostMesh can actually inspect These are proposals, not completed benchmarks or commissioned integrations. Use owned or synthetic tasks, public models, fixed fixtures, and no production credentials. Register scoring rules before examining outputs. Publish failures with successes and retain private inputs separately from a public method. Each experiment should answer a narrower question than whether AI understands everything. Experiment one: match cloud and local model families on the same bounded repository and source-reconciliation tasks. Give each the same allowed tools and input snapshot. Record model versions, hardware limits, latency, total cost, and human repair time; score executable correctness and citation fidelity. Compare against a human baseline and a simple deterministic workflow. This isolates useful task differences without pretending identical tool access eliminates all compute differences. Experiment two: vary horizon while fixing the objective and defining budgets and stopping conditions in advance. Compare one short run with a staged longer run, using caps on elapsed time, tokens, tool calls, and interventions. Stop on completion, exhausted budget, repeated failure, or an authority boundary. Measure verified completion rather than generated volume. Report whether extra runtime repairs earlier errors or compounds them, and whether gains survive on held-out tasks. Experiment three: compare evidence receipts blind. Hide model and operator identities from reviewers, preserve source links and intervention counts, and ask reviewers to reproduce conclusions against the same rubric. Include deliberately unsupported claims and contradictory sources. Agreement without correct rejection is failure. This tests whether a polished artifact or prestigious provider name is masking weak evidence, and whether receipts improve review beyond ordinary answer text. Experiment four: test authority-denials and counterfactual evaluations with synthetic owner-only records and a mock external-action service. Change who is asking while keeping the task wording fixed; then change one decisive source fact while holding the rest constant. Expect unauthorized actions to be denied and factual conclusions to change appropriately. Any unauthorized effect fails the run regardless of task quality. Log denials and permitted completions so blanket refusal cannot masquerade as good governance. Experiment five: teach users the method, then compare public and internal stacks without secrets. Here internal means GhostMesh’s owned orchestration, not a frontier lab. Give participants a short explanation of sources, tools, and verification, then repeat matched tasks with public fixtures and redacted receipts. Test whether calibrated expectations improve and whether stack advantages persist after accounting for assistance. An actual lab comparison would require voluntary, comparable public artifacts; confidential capability claims stay outside the measured result. 8. What would make this thesis wrong? The thesis predicts that task design, access, and verification explain meaningful differences in reported AI experience. It would weaken if matched, repeated evaluations showed no material effect from those factors, or if simple chat and bounded agent workflows delivered equivalent verified outcomes across representative tasks. It would also weaken if blinded reviewers could not gain accuracy from receipts after reasonable training and reproducibility controls. The proposed GhostMesh implementation should be rejected if orchestration adds cost and correlated errors without better completion, if longer horizons merely hide human rescue, or if authority tests fail. A provider advantage that disappears on held-out work should not become an architectural commitment. Consistently superior ordinary workflows are evidence to simplify the system. The point is to invite a result that changes our mind. The funnel remains a useful image for unequal experience, provided it does not become a substitute for evidence. Better public understanding requires portable demonstrations, honest limits, and tasks other people can inspect. GhostMesh should help a reader move from hearing a claim to checking an outcome. That is a more durable contribution than telling the reader how far down an unmeasured population diagram they belong. readers.text: GhostMesh Readers / 003 / October 16, 2026 The Agent a Company Owns A company’s intelligence needs a continuing identity, a bounded mandate, and a record of what it did. An independent GhostMesh reading of Riley Brown’s interview with Vercel founder and CEO Guillermo Rauch. Reader brief What the video is about Riley Brown interviews Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch about V, Eve, reusable skills, tools, memory and a company-owned agent that survives individual conversations. Why you should care Useful for teams considering shared agents. Watch the permission and memory discussion; skip the interview if you need independent productivity measurements or a deployment audit. What GhostMesh takes away Own continuity while proving permission, replay, memory isolation and portability with synthetic tests. A readable agent folder does not itself enforce those boundaries. GhostMesh verdict: Worth studying . Editorial recommendation, not factual verification. Architecture impact: investigate. Proposed only; no adoption implied. Watch on YouTube ↗ The AI Agent Every Company is About to Build | Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch Original interviewer: Riley Brown · Guest: Guillermo Rauch Published August 6, 2026 · 54:22 Original YouTube source ↗ GhostMesh verdict / commentary Own the continuity. Prove the boundaries. An enterprise agent is not a model. It is a governed continuity of identity, memory, delegated capabilities, and accountable action. V offers a compelling organizing idea. Eve offers implementation patterns worth testing. Neither supplies GhostMesh with authority to act. Source navigation Eleven ways into the argument. All 11 creator-provided timestamps, in source order. Why-watch notes are GhostMesh commentary. Each Play here action uses the single player above; original YouTube links work independently. 0:00 Intro Hear the central ambition: a company agent that becomes useful beyond an individual chat session. Original YouTube ↗ 1:21 The State of Agent Adoption Understand why coding becomes a general knowledge-work capability, and where organizational context adds value. Original YouTube ↗ 7:26 ‘V’ Vercel’s Internal Company Agent See how Rauch describes a shared Slack entry point for company knowledge, content, and customer analysis. Original YouTube ↗ 10:18 Building V and the Eve Framework Follow the move from a useful internal assistant to a framework for agents a company can maintain. Original YouTube ↗ 14:32 Lessons from OpenClaw: Soul MD + CPU use Separate editable instructions and a computer’s capabilities from the permissions that must constrain them. Original YouTube ↗ 22:20 One God Agent OR a Team of Agents Examine the tension between one convenient interface and different departments’ rights to information. Original YouTube ↗ 27:11 How to Build Your Own Agent: Skills, Tools & Permissions Follow the concrete distinction between instructions, executable tools, channels, and permission decisions. Original YouTube ↗ 33:52 Proactive Agents, Triggers & Self-Improvement Watch schedules and external events expand the workload, then ask who authorizes the resulting actions. Original YouTube ↗ 40:30 Who Will Build Agents & Getting Started Consider the division between broad contributions to skills and specialist responsibility for data flows and security. Original YouTube ↗ 46:22 The Future: Cheaper, Faster Models & Open Weights Hear the founder’s forecasts about price, speed, and model choice; treat them as forecasts rather than benchmarks. Original YouTube ↗ 53:05 Closing Thoughts: Owning Your Own Intelligence Return to ownership as an organizational identity that should survive a change of model provider. Original YouTube ↗ Independent thesis Interview claims, documented capabilities, and GhostMesh proposals remain separate. Identity and continuity An inspectable company agent The permission gap One door, bounded roles Knowledge that compounds Ownership under change What GhostMesh should consider Evidence ledger and limits Company knowledge becomes a maintained system. The most useful idea in this interview is the shift in where improvement accumulates. An employee can write a better prompt and finish one assignment. A company can instead preserve the procedure, connect it to bounded tools, and make the improvement available to the next employee. That second path creates an institutional asset. Its quality depends on what survives the conversation and who remains responsible for its use. 1. V makes continuity a product question. Rauch describes V as Vercel’s internal company agent, reached through Slack and used for knowledge, customer analysis, and content work. He distinguishes it from the customer-facing support experience. In his account, specialized capabilities sit behind a familiar entry point, with an internal team improving the system. These are founder interview claims, not independently observed deployments or measured productivity results. Watch the V discussion. The important unit is therefore larger than a response. A useful company agent carries definitions, procedures, corrections, and commitments across work. Consider the changelog example: Rauch describes putting his product-marketing judgment into a reusable skill so engineers can explain a shipped improvement in terms customers understand. The organizational gain is the preserved editorial practice, not merely faster drafting. A successor should be able to inspect why that practice exists and revise it when the business changes. For GhostMesh, continuity means retaining an accountable relationship to the Owner across the owner VPS, Hyperion, and Mac. A recurring name alone proves nothing. The working identity needs a stable mandate, traceable changes, and a distinction between proposing work and being authorized to perform it. The same identity can use different models without inheriting new rights from their capabilities. This is an architectural interpretation of the interview, not a claim that V implements GhostMesh’s governance. 2. A folder can make the agent inspectable. Eve’s appeal is its readable shape. The interview describes instructions, executable tools, markdown skills, communication channels, subagents, and schedules. The official repository provides the implementation entry point. The June 17 introduction documents the directory approach, durable sessions, sandboxes, approvals, and delegation. These are documented capabilities; this Reader has not executed them. That arrangement gives reviewers distinct questions to ask. Instructions describe the mandate. Skills encode methods. Tools expose operations. Channels bring in requests and carry results. Subagents divide work, while schedules originate work without a fresh message. Keeping those components visible can make change review more precise: adding a writing guide and adding a publishing credential have very different consequences, even if both appear as small file changes. The soul.md lesson is valuable when understood as explicit behavioral commitments. A prompt can preserve vocabulary, preferred evidence standards, and a rule for acknowledging uncertainty. It does not establish subjective personality, consciousness, or an independent moral authority. Nor does a readable instruction enforce a boundary against a tool that has broader rights. The folder is a review surface; the runtime and connected services must enforce what the prose promises. 3. Approval support leaves a permission gap. Brown identifies a practical difficulty early: sharing a useful skill can accidentally imply sharing access to personal email. Rauch’s later WordPress example makes the issue concrete. An intern may need help drafting without being entitled to publish. His suggestion of delegating to the existing authentication system is a design possibility discussed in the interview, rather than evidence that every Eve installation already enforces that arrangement. Watch skills, tools, and permissions. The current package README calls Eve a preview and assigns safeguard configuration to the deployer. It warns that omitted approval settings can permit tool execution and that sandbox egress is not deny-all. In practical terms, there is no automatic denial to assume. Human approval can be configured; a safe installation requires a complete policy that covers every path to the consequential action. The Agent Stack documentation describes Vercel Connect’s scoped, short-lived tokens. The July 7 GitHub agent guide illustrates runtime credentials and gated writes. Those mechanisms reduce credential exposure and help implement policy. They do not decide whether GhostMesh’s Owner authorized a particular recipient, artifact, or action. A valid service token and an authorized business action are separate facts. 4. One entrance does not require universal access. Rauch favors a unified experience: V routes a request to relevant capabilities instead of making employees memorize every internal tool. Brown presses the counterexample of marketing and finance having different information rights. Both concerns are legitimate. One convenient interface can sit above compartmentalized execution, but only if the router authenticates the caller and preserves that identity throughout delegation. Watch the god-agent debate. A specialist’s clean context is useful but insufficient evidence of isolation. A parent can leak sensitive inputs to a child, a child can return confidential facts to a broad channel, and a shared cache can reintroduce material excluded from the current session. The policy must cover inputs, retrieval, tools, intermediate artifacts, and the final reply. Routing correctness includes declining a request whose answer exists but is outside the caller’s authority. For GhostMesh, Commons should not become a universal context bucket merely because material is easy to retrieve. An Owner-only investigation and a broadly shareable explanation can use the same conceptual vocabulary while retaining different access boundaries. A specialist may inherit a narrower capability set; it should never acquire broader rights because the parent asked persuasively. This is a proposed design constraint, not a verified property of the current mesh. 5. Compounding knowledge needs revision and forgetting. A company agent compounds value when a correction becomes a reusable, source-linked improvement. It compounds error when an attractive answer becomes permanent memory without review. Tony Brain and Library Atlas should be treated as mutable retrieval projections: useful ways to locate and assemble knowledge, with source identities and access labels retained. They should not become immutable authority simply because the same summary appears in several later conversations. Chronology matters. This interview was published August 6. Vercel’s September 9 persistent-memory update documents scoped memory slots and retrieval across sessions. The October 15 Ship recap reports later updates including extensions, dashboard agent creation, and Connect’s general availability. These later primary sources add context; they do not establish that October’s product state existed during the August conversation. GhostMesh should preserve the difference between a source, an interpretation, and a decision. A revised source should make affected interpretations eligible for review. Revoking access should also affect retrieval, derived summaries, and future replies. Improvement is measurable when a corrected definition reaches authorized users while an obsolete or restricted one stops resurfacing. More remembered text alone is not evidence of better institutional knowledge. 6. Ownership has to survive a changed runtime. Rauch argues that model choice lets a company benefit from competition in cost, speed, and capability. His price and performance expectations remain interview forecasts, not benchmarks established here. Model-provider portability is one layer of ownership. Vendor-runtime portability is another: a directory may still depend on hosted workflow state, identity mapping, connector grants, storage, and delivery behavior that do not move with its markdown. There is a concrete reason to test rather than assume lock-in. Vercel’s official self-hosting guide describes building Eve into a Nitro Node service and running it outside Vercel. That route is not a turnkey equivalence guarantee. The operator must supply persistent workflow storage, a compatible sandbox, protected session routes, workflow callback routing, and non-Vercel authentication. Its default local workflow data directory also needs durable storage across process replacement. Thus the portability question is not merely whether a server starts on the VPS; it is whether the same bounded behavior, identity scope, replay outcomes, and recovery guarantees survive a different host without leaking secrets or borrowing production authority. A meaningful portability test would export the agent’s governed state, restore it on an Owner-controlled runtime, and repeat a fixed set of tasks with the same authorization outcomes. The VPS, Hyperion, and Mac offer possible GhostMesh boundaries for such a comparison; this page does not assert that an Eve migration has been attempted. A model swap that preserves fluent answers but drops pending approvals would fail the ownership test. Proactivity raises the stakes. The interview describes schedules, events, and feedback-driven improvement. A trigger establishes that something happened; it does not establish permission to act. Durable replay also does not automatically yield exactly-once external effects. A crash after provider acceptance but before local confirmation can leave the outcome uncertain. GhostMesh needs explicit event identity, bounded authority, and reconciliation before retry, especially for any future delivery path. 7. What GhostMesh should consider These five proposals are classified decisions to investigate, not adopted integrations. All experiments should begin with synthetic data, fake providers, fixed inputs, and no live credentials. Preserve versions and traces so another reviewer can reproduce failures. Successful tests would justify a further Owner review, not commission a service. Borrow / Make the mandate reviewable. Keep instructions, tools, skills, and schedules separately inspectable, with a stable identity record and explicit role boundaries. Risk: readable files create confidence while runtime rights drift. Evidence needed: a manifest mapping each declared capability to enforced access and an attributable change history. Non-adoption criterion: reject any arrangement where a skill edit can silently broaden credentials or where the active mandate cannot be reconstructed. Experiment / Interrupt durable turns and replay. Use a fake delivery service and one-use grant simulator. Interrupt before authorization, after authorization, after simulated acceptance, and before recording confirmation; replay each event ten times. Risk: duplicated effects or stale authority after restart. Pass: one accepted effect per authorized event, zero for expired or reused grants, and uncertain outcomes held for reconciliation. Fail / non-adoption: any duplicate, unauthorized effect, or silent loss of a pending approval. Retain event IDs, state transitions, and provider receipts. Experiment / Challenge identity and memory isolation. Create synthetic Owner, finance, and marketing roles with unique canary facts; test direct requests, parent-to-child delegation, channel changes, and retrieval after revocation.
